outcome: Judged: status rests on Cao & Mehat's September 2026 preprint proving Albertson's conjecture for chromatic number r<=29; Sadhu's all-r v2 claim is set aside as not credible. [Judged 2026-09-28; the researcher's original outcome follows.] A solo-authored September 2026 arXiv preprint (Ankan Sadhu, v2) claims a full proof of Albertson's conjecture for every chromatic number r, superseding an earlier v1 of the same preprint that had claimed only r≤26; a separate concurrent preprint (Cao & Mehat) proves the restricted case r≤29 building on Cranston's r≤24 verification. Neither has been digested by an expert or accepted at a venue; the strongest claim (full proof) rests on a single preprint reviewed only by an automated review tool, not a human expert.

disputes.summary: Sadhu's preprint (arXiv:2609.01682) was posted 2026-09-01 as v1 claiming r≤26 only, then revised 2026-09-13 (v2) to claim a full proof for every r, retitled from 'Albertson's Conjecture Holds for r at Most 26' to 'A Proof of Albertson's Conjecture'. A separate, apparently independent preprint by Cao & Mehat (arXiv:2609.04771, also September 2026) builds on Cranston's r≤24 result and Sadhu's r≤26 result (as of v1) to reach r≤29, without engaging Sadhu's later all-r claim. The two lines of work were not reconciled in any source found, and no expert commentary distinguishing/adjudicating between them was located.

summary: At the frozen revision the conjecture was verified for r≤18 (Albertson-Cranston-Fox for r≤12, Barát-Tóth for r≤16, Ackerman for r≤18). Since then, several independent lines of work have pushed the verified range and one preprint claims a full resolution. (1) Daniel Cranston (arXiv:2512.08020, submitted 2025-12-08, no AI disclosure) verified r≤24 and restricted possible counterexamples for r∈{25,26} to three residual orders. (2) Jacob Fox, János Pach and Andrew Suk (arXiv:2510.05893, SoCG 2025 version at drops.dagstuhl.de/.../LIPIcs.SoCG.2025.50, no AI disclosure) proved a genuinely restricted case: graphs of chromatic number k with at most 1.4(k-1) vertices satisfy Albertson's conjecture (via a weak-immersion argument going through the related Lescure-Meyniel conjecture), for k sufficiently large — this is a case, not a range-of-r extension, and does not itself resolve any full r. (3) Ankan Sadhu, solo author (arXiv:2609.01682), first posted 2026-09-01 as 'Albertson's Conjecture Holds for r at Most 26' (a case extension eliminating Cranston's residual r∈{25,26} orders), then revised 2026-09-13 into 'A Proof of Albertson's Conjecture' claiming the full conjecture for every r, using Gallai decomposition, weak-immersion routing near r, and exact-certificate verification for a middle range, with 'exact verification certificates archived on GitHub and Zenodo.' The paper discloses that ChatGPT was used only for literature search, language editing and verification assistance, with the author stating he takes responsibility for all mathematical content — this is not AI-generated mathematics under the coding rules, so ai_role is none. (4) Sen Cao and Sanjit Singh Mehat (arXiv:2609.04771, September 2026) independently extended Cranston's r≤24 plus the (v1) r≤26 result to r≤29 using Kempe-chain/immersion, Gallai join structure and Tutte-barrier arguments; their AI disclosure states generative AI/LLMs were used 'substantially' for 'mathematical exploration, intermediate checking, and manuscript drafting,' again with the human authors claiming full responsibility — again coded none under the rule that checking, drafting-assistance and exploration-suggestion by itself does not make the role assisted or generated, since no specific piece of mathematics in the result is attributed to the AI by the authors. (5) Separately, the AI-agent research platform ProofAtlas hosts a live 'collaboration' workspace on this conjecture where AI agents pursue a 'globally minimal-counterexample' framework and report (unaudited, 'source-reported', explicitly marked unreproduced) analytic exclusion results for r≥5446 and adjacent exact-integer exclusions for r=5442-5445; an independent reader's guide to the platform explicitly warns that 'accepted in ProofAtlas' is not peer review and such claims should be treated 'as a lead, not a fact.' None of the ProofAtlas-internal claims have been published, checked by a human, or corroborated elsewhere, so they are not counted as an event here. Because Sadhu's full-r claim is only weeks old, solo-authored, and has so far been read only by an automated review tool (pith.science's 'Pith Review', itself an AI system, not a mathematician) rather than any named expert, journal, or the authors of the competing r≤29 paper, the overall status is coded claimed rather than resolved. The r≤24/26/29 case-extension work, taken on its own, would be coded partial, but the later, broader claim supersedes it as the decisive event for this record per instructions to describe the decisive event and note the others.
competing_reading: If one instead treats Sadhu's all-r claim as not yet a serious enough claim to be the decisive event (given it is solo-authored, unreviewed by any named mathematician, and its own v1/v2 history shows the scope ballooning within two weeks from r≤26 to 'all r' with no apparent independent check), the decisive event could instead be read as the r≤29 case-extension (Cao & Mehat / Cranston lineage), giving status partial with resolution_direction confirmed for the r≤29 range and leaving the general conjecture open. Under that reading ai_role is still none for the same disclosure reasons. I judged claimed to be the more faithful code because a full-scope proof claim exists in the primary literature dated within the window and 'claimed' is explicitly the status for exactly this situation (preprint or announcement not yet digested), rather than silently downgrading a found claim to a weaker status.
what_would_settle_it: A human expert digestion (a referee report, a blog post from a specialist in crossing numbers/chromatic graph theory such as Cranston, Fox, Pach, Suk, or Tóth, or journal acceptance) of Sadhu's arXiv:2609.01682 v2 either endorsing or finding an error in the all-r proof; alternatively, a retraction, a v3 narrowing the claim again, or a published refutation would settle it the other way.

If a named expert endorses it, status becomes resolved. Cao-Mehat's 'mathematical exploration' LLM use could hide AI-produced content, but no specific piece is attributed to AI, so kept none. The r<=29 result partly relies on Sadhu v1's r<=26 step.
